paras: The attempted lynching of Tom Herbert was an attack by a mob on the jail at Kernville, Kern County, California, on the night of October 18, 1881, intended to seize and hang Herbert, a prisoner charged with murdering the mine owner who had employed him. Deputy Sheriff Ben Mitchell, who met the mob short of the jail, was shot dead, and his return fire wounded one of the attackers, Jim Cochran. The mob dispersed without reaching Herbert, and Bakersfield dispatches carried the story as far as Chicago and Memphis.

Herbert worked at a mine on Piute Mountain, about twenty-five miles from Havilah, owned by Charles Ziegler and a partner named Scodie. According to an October 20 dispatch, the two quarreled the previous Thursday, and Ziegler paid Herbert off and dismissed him before a Frenchman who later disappeared. The next morning Herbert told a neighbor that Ziegler was dead, and the body was found with three bullet wounds.

Justice Goodale of Havilah, acting as coroner, held an inquest at which Herbert was the only witness. Herbert testified that they had been drinking and that he woke to find Ziegler dead, and he explained the blood on his trousers and boots by saying the body had lain across them. A constable then arrested Herbert and lodged him in the jail at Kernville, charged with the murder.

On the night of October 18 a mob of fifteen or twenty men, most of them reportedly drunk, started for the Kernville jail to hang Herbert. Mitchell intercepted them about one hundred yards from the jail, and a telephone dispatch from Kernville added that he refused to surrender his prisoner. The mob shot him in the stomach with a shotgun and in the left shoulder blade with a pistol.

Before he fell, Mitchell fired his gun, loaded with buckshot, and hit Jim Cochran in the right breast; Cochran was said to be the man who had shot the officer. The mob then dispersed, leaving Herbert "still safe in jail," and the sheriff and a posse left Bakersfield for Kernville.

By October 27 eleven people were under arrest and warrants were out for nine more. Those brought to Bakersfield included John Hutchings, David Applegate, Bruce Landers and J. Bremeier. On October 31 Herbert was examined before Justice Wilkinson and held without bail on the murder charge, and Cochran was brought to the Bakersfield jail the same day.

The examination of eleven accused mob members ran from Monday to November 4, when all were discharged except J. Cochran, who was held to answer for murder. The evidence was called "tolerably clear" that Cochran fired one of the two fatal shots, and his wound had led to his identification. Cochran and Herbert were then both in the county jail awaiting the Superior Court, and no report of either man's trial appears in the coverage through November.

The story traveled as Bakersfield wire dispatches, first in California and Nevada dailies and then in Chicago, Memphis, Salt Lake City, Butte and Midwestern weeklies. California papers framed it chiefly as the killing of an officer: the Sacramento Daily Record-Union headed its first report "Killed in the Performance of His Duty" and its full account "Deputy Sheriff Killed by a Mob," paired with "Mine Owner Murdered by his Employee." The Chicago Daily Tribune ran the San Francisco wire under "Judge Lynch in Disgrace," and the Los Angeles Herald described the affair as "murderous lynching demonstrations."

Several reports stated Herbert's guilt as fact before any trial, calling him "the murderer" or the man "who killed Seigler," while the Sacramento paper called the wounded Cochran "the Vigillante." Early digests garbled the wounded man's name as "Tom Canty" or "Tim Carby" and called him mortally wounded; later dispatches named him Jim Cochran, recovering. None of the reports stated the race of Herbert, Ziegler, Mitchell or the men in the mob.

The first full Bakersfield dispatch put the mob at fifteen or twenty men, while the telephone dispatch from Kernville the same day put it at twenty-five to forty. Most reports, including the dispatch written the next day, placed the attack on the night of October 18, but the November 4 dispatch dated it the 19th.

accounts.label: Telephone dispatch from Kernville

accounts.label: San Francisco wire

accounts.label: Examination of accused mob members
accounts.gist: Of eleven men examined, only J. Cochran was identified, by his wound, as having fired one of the two fatal shots and was held for murder.

framing.detail: California dispatches centered the slain officer: 'Killed in the Performance of His Duty'; the LA Herald called it 'murderous lynching demonstrations.'
The Chicago Daily Tribune headed the wire 'Judge Lynch in Disgrace.'
Memphis, Butte, Salt Lake and Midwestern weeklies ran the San Francisco wire or digest without comment.
While faulting the mob, reports presented the accused as guilty: 'the murderer, Thomas Hebert', 'who killed Seigler', 'Mine Owner Murdered by his Employee'.
